Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Bao, a 31-year-old carpenter, sits stiffly in the waiting room chair, positioning it so he can see both the door to the office and the entrance to the clinic. It has been eight months since the traffic stop, but the feeling of being exposed, of imminent danger, has become a permanent feature of his life. The incident itself began with something mundane: a burned-out tail light. He remembers the flashing lights appearing in his rearview mirror and the familiar, mild annoyance of being pulled over. But this time was different. The two officers took his license and registration and returned to their car. Five minutes turned into ten, then fifteen. With each passing minute, a cold dread bloomed in Bao’s chest. He was certain that the delay meant something terrible was about to happen; they must have found something, mistaken him for someone else, or were simply deciding what to do with him.

When they finally emerged and strode toward his car, their movements were tense and aggressive. They ordered him out of the vehicle. Before he could fully process the command, his door was pulled open and he was hauled out onto the pavement. One officer held his arms behind his back, pressing his face into the cold metal of his own truck, while the other began to search him. Pinned and unable to see, all he could hear was the rustling of their uniforms and their low, menacing voices. He felt utterly powerless. A question escaped his lips—"What did I do?"—and the pressure on his back intensified, a knee driving into his spine as his head was slammed against the side panel of the truck. The world went blurry with a flash of pain. They found nothing, issued a ticket for the tail light, and left him shaking by the side of the road.

In the weeks that followed, Bao’s world began to shrink. At home, he found he could no longer sit on the couch with his wife if his back was to the door; he felt a prickling unease, a certainty that he was vulnerable. He started taking the seat at the end of the dinner table, the one against the wall. He told his wife it was more comfortable, but the truth was that any other position felt intolerably unsafe. This vigilance followed him to work. During client meetings or lunch breaks with his crew, he would subtly maneuver himself into a corner, needing to see everyone and everything. He was unable to relax, even in the quiet of his own home on a Sunday afternoon. His body remained coiled tight, as if anticipating a blow that never came.

The rumination was relentless. He replayed the traffic stop endlessly, dissecting his every word and action. He became convinced that if he had just been more compliant, quieter, or had not asked what he had done, the violence would not have happened. He repeatedly blamed himself for what happened, believing his own behavior had provoked the officers. This shame was a constant, heavy companion. To escape it, and the ever-present hum of anxiety, he tried to actively push away any thought of the event. When a siren wailed in the distance or the memory of the cold metal against his cheek surfaced, he would immediately blast music in his workshop or start a frantic, unnecessary task. When that failed, usually in the quiet of the evening, he began to take drugs he bought from a coworker, finding a temporary, hazy silence in the high.

This has taken its toll. Delays, once a simple annoyance of the construction trade, now trigger panic. When a lumber delivery is an hour late, his mind doesn't just worry about the project timeline; he becomes certain that something catastrophic has occurred, that the truck has crashed or the supplier has cheated him, sending him into a spiral of agitation. His wife’s patience has worn thin with his constant tension, his catastrophic thinking when she’s late from the grocery store, and his increasing reliance on drugs to get through the week. It was after she found his stash and confronted him, her voice trembling with fear and exhaustion, that Bao knew he could not continue this way. He came to therapy not with hope, but with a desperate fear that he was losing everything: his marriage, his business, and the man he used to be before that night on the side of the road.
